title: After the JD III: Third Results from a National Study of Legal Careers
pub: American Bar Foundation / NALP Foundation for Law Career Research and Education
author: Gabriele Plickert · Ronit Dinovitzer · Bryant G. Garth · Robert L. Nelson · Rebecca Sandefur · Joyce Sterling · David B. Wilkins

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source contains no substantive natural-language claims and lacks interpretable table context, so there is insufficient evidence to determine its position on multidisciplinary implementation, verification, task-specific evaluation, or reliable legal-service delivery.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source documents pre-AI career mobility, satisfaction and unequal recession effects, but does not address legal AI, jagged capability, verification, selective deployment or operating-model redesign. Its labour-market evidence may provide historical context, but it does not establish a position on the cluster’s proposition.

st.t: Legal careers: Mobility coexists with sector barriers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core account of structured mobility and materially develops it with longitudinal evidence that starting sector constrains later destinations, while documenting persistent gender disparities, career-stage turnover, movement away from firms, and measurement limits.
qs: For example, very few lawyers who start in solo or small firm practice move into larger private firms, however, some do move into state government positions.
However, contrary to hopes, if not expectations, the gap between the earnings of women and men has continued and, in fact, has grown since Wave 2.

st.t: Big Law economics: Durable value exceeds firm size
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s account of Big Law as economically resilient yet vulnerable to demand shocks and partner-profit pressures. Its respondent reports document layoffs, reduced hiring and delayed partnership promotion, while its qualified explanation links large-firm staffing cuts to both lower demand and preserving partner profits; it does not predict large-firm disappearance.
qs: About half of the respondents in large law firms reported their employers laid off lawyers and support personnel, over 30% reported an increase in the time for promotion to partnership, and 55% reported reduced overall hiring.
The incentives to lay off lawyers and support personnel were likely higher in the larger law firms seeking to cut costs not only in response to lower demand but also to maintain partner profits.

st.t: Career inequality: Professional change preserves unequal rewards
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition by documenting stable, high career-choice satisfaction alongside continuing gender inequality. Its declining-mobility finding also aligns with the cluster’s cautious treatment of mobility, without establishing that professional hierarchy has become fixed.
qs: Twelve years into their careers, 76% of the  16  After the JD III: Third Results of a National Study of Legal Careers  6(&7,21^C^T  respondents report that they are moderately or extremely satisfied with their decision to become a lawyer, a proportion virtually unchanged from prior waves of the survey.

st.t: Graduate hiring: Strong outcomes mask entry contraction
st.an: The source indirectly supports the synthesis by documenting that substantial hiring retrenchment occurred before generative AI and by showing that aggregate career outcomes remained stratified by educational credentials. It therefore reinforces the cluster’s caution against attributing current entry-level contraction to AI alone and its qualification that market resilience does not imply equal access.
qs: About half of the respondents in large law firms reported their employers laid off lawyers and support personnel, over 30% reported an increase in the time for promotion to partnership, and 55% reported reduced overall hiring.
Lawyers from the most highly ranked law schools continue to work disproportionately in the most lucrative legal settings and, consequently, continue to earn higher incomes.

st.t: Research representation: Purposeful samples limit wider claims
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s emphasis on participant composition and limits on wider or longitudinal claims. It reports racial and ethnic career patterns while explicitly warning that cross-wave differences partly reflect changes in who responded, rather than solely individual career transitions.
qs: Comparisons across waves, such as those in Table 2.1, are, unless otherwise noted, based on comparing responses from whoever answered the survey in a specific wave.
Thus, some of the differences across waves reflect the fact that a different set of respondents participated in the three waves of the study.

kp.k: Longitudinal evidence tracks the 2000 entry cohort
kp.d: The study follows lawyers admitted in 2000 at approximately three, seven and twelve years into their careers. AJD3 collected data from May 2012 to early 2013, reporting 2,862 complete surveys: 53% of previous respondents and about 35% of the initial eligible sample of 8,225. These are historical findings on careers and recession effects, not claims about AI.
qs: After the JD was designed to track the careers of a nationally representative cohort of lawyers admitted to the bar in the year 2000 over the first 12 years of their careers.
In total, AJD3 obtained complete surveys from 2,862 respondents, for a response rate of 53% of individuals who previously responded to either AJD1 or AJD2.
This amounts to a response rate of about 35 percent of the initial sample of 8,225 established in 2002.

kp.k: Cross-wave comparisons require sample-composition qualifications
kp.d: Unless otherwise specified, comparisons use whoever responded in each wave rather than an identical panel. The report therefore cautions that apparent changes can reflect differential participation. Most sections use the weighted national sample, while Section 9 includes the minority oversample. The authors report limited observed nonresponse differences but acknowledge that further analysis is needed.
qs: Thus, some of the differences across waves reflect the fact that a different set of respondents participated in the three waves of the study.
The findings in this report represent the national sample of respondents, except Section 9, which includes the minority oversample.

While these results provide a broad overview about AJD respondents’ careers and personal pathways, further research and multivariate analyses will be important to better understand the dynamics of lawyers’ careers.

kp.k: Careers shift from law firms toward business
kp.d: Private law firms employed about 70% of respondents in Wave 1 but 48.5% in Wave 3; the public sector employed 28% and business 20% in Wave 3. The business share rose from about 8% at entry to 19% in Wave 2. Business employment encompasses both in-house legal practice and non-practising positions, with just over one third of business respondents not practising law.
qs: At Wave 3, which is the 12-year career milestone, we found 48.5% of respondents working in the private law firm sector, 28% working in the public sector, and 20% working in business (with another 3.5% indicating working in “other” settings).
While only 8% of AJD respondents began their careers in business, by Wave 2, those working in this sector grew to 19% and, in Wave 3, to 20%.
Of AJD respondents working in the business sector, just over one third were not practicing law.

kp.k: Large-firm participation declines as careers mature
kp.d: The share working in firms with more than 250 lawyers fell from about 18% in Wave 1 to 8.3% in Wave 3. Solo and small-firm representation remained virtually unchanged between Waves 2 and 3. The report situates this change around partnership decisions and the economic downturn without establishing their separate causal contributions.
qs: the proportion of AJD lawyers in large law firms (> 250) showed the greatest decline since AJD respondents had begun their careers, from a high of about 18 percent at Wave 1 to 8.3% at Wave 3.
Most private firm lawyers responding to AJD3 worked at smaller firms of 2–20 lawyers, with the next largest group in solo practice.

kp.k: Non-practice careers and reduced full-time participation persist
kp.d: In Wave 3, 19.2% were not practising law, compared with approximately 15% in Wave 1; men and women, and White and minority lawyers, were about equally likely to work outside legal practice. Full-time employment declined from 93.6% in Wave 1 to 85.8% in Wave 3. The authors suggest both economic contraction and caregiving-related labour-force changes contributed.
qs: By the third wave of the survey, about a fifth of this cohort of lawyers (19.2%) were not practicing law
Men and women were equally likely to be working outside the practice of law in the third wave.
White and minority lawyers were about equally likely to be working outside the practice of law.

kp.k: Long working hours vary substantially by setting
kp.d: Among full-time workers, median weekly hours were 47 overall and 53 in the largest firms. Some 15.3% worked more than 60 hours weekly. Such exceptionally long weeks became less common across employment settings as respondents entered mid-career, but remained more prevalent in private practice.
qs: The median AJD3 attorney works 47 hours a week, seven hours longer than a traditional full-time job of 40 hours per week.
According to Wave 3 respondents, the longest hours are worked by lawyers in the largest firms, with a median of 53 hours per week.
The share of AJD lawyers working more than 60 hours per week has declined across all employment settings as these lawyers have entered mid-career

kp.k: Specialist identity differs from actual work concentration
kp.d: Self-identification as a specialist increased from 39.4% in Wave 1 to 54.3% in Wave 2 and 66.3% in Wave 3. However, the proportion spending at least half their time in one field declined from 85.6% in Wave 2 to 75.5% in Wave 3. These measures distinguish professional self-description from reported allocation of work.
qs: About two thirds (66.3%) of AJD3 lawyers identify themselves as specialists in their work.
In AJD3, about three quarters (75.5%) of attorneys report working at least half of their time in a single area of law.
The attorneys least likely to report spending half their time in one field are public interest lawyers and lawyers working for the federal government.

kp.k: Pro bono participation masks highly uneven contributions
kp.d: Some 55.1% reported pro bono activity. Among participants, mean annual service was 62.2 hours, exceeding the ABA Model Rule 6.1 aspirational standard of 50 hours, but the median was only 25. Smaller-firm lawyers devoted more hours on average to poor and low-income clients, whereas larger-firm lawyers devoted more to charitable organisations.
qs: Somewhat over half (55.1%) of the lawyers in the third wave of the AJD report were engaging in pro bono activities.
However, median hours among those who did pro bono service were 25 per year.

Lawyers working in smaller firms, on average, devoted more hours to the service of poor and low-income clients while lawyers in larger firms, on average, devoted more hours to charitable organizations.

kp.k: Nominal income growth conceals widening earnings dispersion
kp.d: Full-time respondents' median compensation reached $106,000, approximately 8% above Wave 2 without inflation adjustment. The lower-quartile threshold fell from $70,000 in 2006 to $60,000 in 2011, while the upper-quartile threshold rose from $145,000 to $171,000. The authors suggest, rather than demonstrate, that the crisis disproportionately affected precarious earners.
qs: Across the sample, median earnings were up 8% unadjusted for inflation, with half of AJD3 respondents (working full time) earning more than $106,000 and half earning less.
The highest earning quarter started at $171,000 in 2011, up from $145,000 in 2006.

kp.k: Practice setting and educational credentials remain earnings correlates
kp.d: The largest firms had the highest reported median compensation at $225,000. Graduates of highly ranked schools remained disproportionately represented in lucrative settings, and higher self-reported GPAs generally correlated with higher earnings across schools. Table 5.2 uses unweighted data; these descriptive relationships do not isolate causal effects of credentials.
qs: Lawyers in firms of more than 251 lawyers were earning a median salary of $225,000, the highest median salary of all settings.
Lawyers from the most highly ranked law schools continue to work disproportionately in the most lucrative legal settings and, consequently, continue to earn higher incomes.
Across all law schools, with few exceptions, higher GPAs are related to higher earnings.

kp.k: Compensation sources differ across organisational settings
kp.d: Salary remained the main income source across sectors. Among bonus recipients, the median bonus was $15,000, with the largest reported bonuses in business legal practice at $30,000. Profit sharing mattered in both the largest firms and solo or small practices; stock options were reported almost exclusively in business.
qs: Salaries continue to represent the bulk of lawyers’ incomes across all sectors.
The median bonus, as indicated by those who reported receiving bonuses, was $15,000.
However, it is clear that profit sharing is also an important source of income among those in solo and small firms.

kp.k: Career satisfaction stays high despite setting-specific trade-offs
kp.d: Approximately 76% remained moderately or extremely satisfied with becoming lawyers. Satisfaction was especially high in public interest and legal services/public defence, but only 63.4% among business respondents not practising law. Large-firm respondents reported comparatively low job-setting satisfaction, while the largest-firm respondents rated compensation and advancement more positively. Solo and small-firm respondents reported relatively strong satisfaction across multiple dimensions.
qs: The Wave 3 data show that, 12 years into their careers, most lawyers (76%) reported they were moderately or extremely satisfied with their decision to become a lawyer, a proportion virtually unchanged from prior waves of the survey.

As in the previous reports, the lowest job setting satisfaction was expressed by respondents in the large law firms, led by firms of 101–250 lawyers, followed closely by respondents in the largest law firms.
However mixed the category, the Wave 3 solos and those working in small firms were generally relatively satisfied compared to their peers in other settings across all dimensions of satisfaction.

kp.k: Job mobility slows but remains substantial
kp.d: Between 2007 and 2013, 36% changed jobs at least once, compared with 62% between 2003 and 2007 in Section 7. Intended job changes fell from 32.5% to 23.9%. Public interest lawyers had particularly high actual and intended mobility; the report separately cautions that mobility intentions do not straightforwardly indicate dissatisfaction.
qs: In Wave 2, 62% of lawyers had changed jobs at least once between 2003 and 2007.
By contrast, as Table 7.1a shows, between 2007 and 2013, 36% of lawyers changed jobs at least once.
It is important to recall mobility intentions are not a straightforward indicator of dissatisfaction

kp.k: Early practice settings shape later career destinations
kp.d: For respondents participating in both Waves 1 and 3, continued presence in the same setting varied markedly: 55% for state government, 53% for inside counsel and about 19% for firms of 101–250 lawyers. Few starting in solo or small firms moved into larger firms. Entry into in-house roles by mid-career was more common for those starting in-house or in larger firms.
qs: Where lawyers start also influences where they can go later in their careers.
For example, very few lawyers who start in solo or small firm practice move into larger private firms, however, some do move into state government positions.
Lawyers are far more likely to gain a position as an inside counsel in business by mid-career if they started as inside counsel or worked in a larger private law firm ( 101-250, or 251+) .

kp.k: Gender gaps widen in earnings and partnership advancement
kp.d: The report describes the earnings gap rising from 5% after two to three years to 15% after seven years and 20% after twelve. Full-time median incomes were $106,000 for women and $132,000 for men. Men were more likely to become partners and equity partners; women were more likely to hold non-equity partnerships. Public-sector earnings gaps were substantially narrower.
qs: After only 2 to 3 years of practice, women and men had a 5% gap in income.
By Wave 2, after 7 years, that gap had increased to 15%, and now after 12 years of practice, the overall gap is 20%.
In fact, we see that men were more likely to have been promoted to partner and were more likely to have become equity partners than women at the same stage.
Women in the public sector made between 96% and 98% of men’s incomes for comparable positions.

kp.k: Parenthood affects women's labour-force participation disproportionately
kp.d: The report associates childcare with women's greater likelihood of part-time work or non-employment, reporting 15% part-time and 9% not currently working, while 96% of men worked full-time. Fewer women reported altering professional lives because of children between Waves 2 and 3; the suggestion that children were reaching school age is explicitly tentative.
qs: Women were significantly more likely to indicate they are part time (15%) or not currently working (9%) to care for children.
For men, the same phenomena rarely occur (96% of men were working full time).
Perhaps they had begun to enter the family lifecycle in which children were beginning to go to school.

kp.k: Racial groups experience different sectoral career trajectories
kp.d: Using the joint national/minority sample, the report finds just over one third of Black lawyers in private firms and 42% in government and public-sector work. Asian lawyers' private-firm share fell to 38.4%, while 31.4% worked in government or public-sector jobs and 27.5% in business. Hispanic private-firm participation was 45.6%, versus 50.2% for White lawyers. These are cohort-specific descriptive distributions.
qs: The largest decline in private law firm practice was experienced by Asian lawyers.
While almost half of Asian lawyers worked in law firms at Wave 2, only 38.4% remained in this sector at Wave 3.
Across the sample, Asian (27.5%) lawyers are most likely to be working in business, with Hispanics least likely to be working in this sector (15.3%).

kp.k: Debt repayment progresses unevenly across racial groups
kp.d: The reported debt-free share rose from 16.3% in Wave 1 to 36.1% in Wave 2 and 47.4% in Wave 3. Only 23.3% of Black and 30.4% of Hispanic respondents reported zero debt, compared with 60.1% of Asian respondents and approximately 48% of White respondents. Among Hispanic respondents with debt, the median rose from $60,000 to $75,000. The report cautions that minority counts without the oversample are small; debt medians exclude zero balances.
qs: For the sample as a whole, the percentage with zero debt increased over the three waves from 16.3% at Wave 1 to 36.1% at Wave 2 to almost half (47.4%) at Wave 3.
Only 23.3% of Blacks reported zero debt compared with 30.4% of Hispanics, 60.1% of Asians, and 48% of Whites.
The median excludes individuals who reported zero debt.

kp.k: Debt findings do not establish continuing subjective impacts
kp.d: Earlier AJD analyses found little relationship between remaining debt and career satisfaction or perceived educational value, with moderate effects on home purchase. Wave 3 did not ask about continuing debt impacts, so its findings concern repayment metrics rather than whether debt still influenced career choices or satisfaction. Debt-free shares were comparatively high in several public-sector and business settings as well as large firms.
qs: Unfortunately, because of our focus in Wave 3 on the impact of the recession and the fact that debt recedes in importance over time for most lawyers, the Wave 3 survey did not ask respondents about the continuing impact of educational debt.
Our discussion thus focuses on the basic metrics of student loan debt repayment.
Those least likely to have paid down their debt completely were working in solo practice, state government, and legal services or public defender settings.

kp.k: Recession effects were uneven across individual careers
kp.d: Respondents reported no noticeable personal effect in 42% of cases and positive effects in almost 7%; 24% experienced reduced compensation, 12% changed jobs, 10% experienced loan-repayment effects and 5% lost jobs. The authors propose that established skills, clients and connections may have buffered this experienced cohort, contrasting it with reported entry-level hardship rather than directly studying new entrants.
qs: When asked to consider the impact of the recession on their individual careers, 42% reported no noticeable effect, and almost 7% reported a positive effect.
It may be that being 8 or more years into their careers at the time of the downturn afforded them sufficient skills, clients, and connections to weather the recession
However, only 5% lost their jobs.

kp.k: Recession pressures differed by setting, gender and race
kp.d: Solo and small-firm respondents reported particularly strong income pressure: 35.8% reported income cuts and 18.1% loan-repayment effects. In large firms, 18% reported delayed promotion. Women there reported more layoffs and removal from partnership tracks than men, despite men reporting more delayed or denied promotions. Black respondents reported a 14.4% layoff rate overall, while Black and Hispanic respondents more often reported loan-repayment difficulties.
qs: In that group, 35.8% reported a cut in income.
Those working in large law firms predictably reported the strongest effects on their success in terms of the partnership track, with 18% reporting that the recession delayed promotion
Black respondents were the most likely to report they had been laid off because of the recession (14.4%).

kp.k: Employers absorbed shocks through staffing and compensation changes
kp.d: Respondents reported employer business downturns in 43.2% of cases, reduced hiring in 37.7%, pay freezes in 35.9%, support-personnel layoffs in 25.4% and lawyer layoffs in 16.5%. About half of large-firm respondents reported lawyer and support-staff layoffs, and 55% reported reduced hiring. These are respondents' reports about workplaces, not a separately sampled census of employers. The authors suggest maintaining partner profits, alongside lower demand, encouraged larger-firm cost cutting.
qs: On the other hand, 43.2% of AJD respondents reported their employers experienced a downturn in business, and 16.5% reported their employers laid off attorneys.
In general, the leading effects among the employers were reduced hiring (37.7 %), pay freezes (35.9 %), and lay-offs of support personnel (25.4%).
The incentives to lay off lawyers and support personnel were likely higher in the larger law firms seeking to cut costs not only in response to lower demand but also to maintain partner profits.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: No AI-related claims or predictions are present.
pts.d: The report examines lawyers’ career trajectories, practice settings, earnings, satisfaction, mobility, inequality, educational debt, and experiences of the economic recession. It does not attribute changes in legal services or lawyers’ careers to AI. Its historical findings should not be recast as AI predictions.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: No evidence is offered for AI-driven change.
pts.d: The source provides longitudinal survey evidence about legal careers, not evidence about AI adoption or effects. The introduction reports 2,862 completed surveys for the third wave; these data do not support any AI claim made by the source, because none is made.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: No AI-related timeframe or conditions are specified.
pts.d: Published in 2014, the report covers a cohort admitted to the bar in 2000, with survey waves in 2002–2003, 2007–2008, and 2012–2013. These are historical observation periods, not forecasts of AI transformation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: No group is identified as affected by AI.
pts.d: The report distinguishes lawyers by practice setting, firm size, gender, race and ethnicity, and educational background. Reported differences concern career development and economic conditions, not AI-related impacts on these groups.
